pages.name: Three meters
pages.text: An example bench: a 6 Ω resistor and an ideal 25.5 mH coil in series on a 20 V, 50 Hz supply. Like ordinary AC meters, the voltmeters read rms, and one current, 2 A, flows through both parts. The meter across the resistor reads 12 V and the one across the coil 16 V. Added as plain numbers that makes 28 V, yet the supply's meter reads only 20 V.

pages.name: Where did 8 V go?
pages.task: The two parts share one current, yet their 12 V and 16 V make only 20 V on the supply's meter, not 28 V. Why?
pages.answer: The two voltages peak a quarter cycle apart
pages.why: At every instant the supply's voltage is the resistor's plus the coil's, just as on DC. But the resistor's voltage is in step with the current, and the coil's peaks a quarter cycle earlier (lessons 3 and 4). When one is at its peak the other is passing through zero, so they are never both at full size together. Their sum peaks at 28.3 V, not 17.0 V + 22.6 V, and 28.3 V peak is 20 V rms. An ideal coil takes no watts, so nothing is lost as heat, and one series loop carries one current.

pages.name: Tip to tail
pages.text: As in Trigonometry lesson 7, each wave becomes an arrow, here as long as its meter reading. The current is the reference, so it lies flat. V_R lies flat with it, because a resistor's voltage is in step with its current. V_L points straight up, a quarter turn ahead, because the coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle earlier. Laid tip to tail they make a right-angled triangle. Its closing side, √(12² + 16²) = 20 V, swings down onto the supply meter's reading. The angle φ is the [[phase angle]], how far the supply's voltage leads the current.

pages.name: A second bench
pages.task: Another resistor and coil in series: 10 V across the resistor and 24 V across the coil. What does the supply's meter read?
pages.why: Lay the arrows tip to tail: 10 V flat and 24 V straight up. The supply's voltage is the closing side, √(10² + 24²) = √676 = 26 V. 34 V adds them as plain numbers, as if they peaked together. 14 V takes one from the other, as if they peaked half a cycle apart.

pages.name: Divide by the current
pages.text: Every side of the triangle is a voltage, and the same 2 A flows through every part. Divide each side by 2 A and it becomes an opposition in ohms: 12 V becomes R = 6 Ω, 16 V becomes X_L = 8 Ω, and 20 V becomes the circuit's whole opposition to AC, its [[impedance]], Z = 10 Ω. The triangle shrinks but keeps its shape and its angle, because every side is divided by the same number. So Z = √(R² + X_L²), and I = V ÷ Z.

pages.name: On the mains
pages.task: A resistor and a coil in series on 230 V, 50 Hz mains. The ammeter reads 5 A and the meter across the resistor 200 V. What are the resistance R and the coil's reactance X_L?
pages.why: Divide each reading by the 5 A. The resistor's 200 V gives R = 40 Ω, the flat side, and the supply's 230 V gives Z = 46 Ω, the closing side. The coil's side is the upright: X_L = √(46² − 40²) = √516 ≈ 22.7 Ω, and its hidden meter reads √(230² − 200²) ≈ 113.6 V. 6 Ω takes 200 V from 230 V as plain numbers and divides the 30 V by 5 A. 46 Ω takes the whole circuit's impedance as the coil's reactance.

pages.name: Slide the frequency
pages.text: The supply stays at 20 V while the frequency plays up to 100 Hz, down to 0 Hz and back to 50 Hz. R stays put, but X_L = 2πfL grows with the frequency, so the triangle stands taller as it rises and lies flat on R at 0 Hz, steady DC. That is why an ohmmeter, whose steady current makes no back-emf, reads only a coil's R. A real coil is a resistance and an ideal coil in one body, drawn dashed, and the last rows find its inductance. Slide the frequency or the resistance yourself.

pages.name: An unknown coil
pages.task: An unknown coil reads 8 Ω on an ohmmeter. On a 34 V, 50 Hz test supply it draws 2 A. What is its inductance?
pages.why: The AC meters give Z = 34 V ÷ 2 A = 17 Ω, the closing side. The ohmmeter gives R = 8 Ω, the flat side. The upright is X_L = √(17² − 8²) = 15 Ω, and L = 15 ÷ (2π × 50) = 47.7 mH. 54.1 mH takes all 17 Ω as reactance and forgets the wire's resistance. 28.6 mH takes 8 Ω from 17 Ω as plain numbers, leaving 9 Ω.

pages.name: Swap in a capacitor
pages.text: Back on the first bench, the coil is swapped for a 398 µF capacitor, whose reactance at 50 Hz is also 8 Ω. The meters still read 12 V, 16 V and 20 V, but a capacitor's voltage peaks a quarter cycle after its current (lesson 5), so its arrow, V_C, points straight down. The triangle flips below the line and φ reads −53.13°: the supply's voltage lags the current. Here the triangle is drawn in volts, with the supply's side held at 20 V, so V_C shrinks and grows with X_C. Then the frequency plays up to 100 Hz: X_C shrinks to 4 Ω and φ reads −33.7°. Slide it down to 5 Hz, where X_C is 80 Ω and the triangle stands almost on end.

pages.name: Name the ohms
pages.task: From the first bench: the ohmmeter reads 6 Ω across the resistor. 16 V ÷ 2 A = 8 Ω across the coil, and 8 Ω across the capacitor. 20 V ÷ 2 A = 10 Ω across the supply. Which naming is right?
pages.answer: Resistance 6 Ω, reactances 8 Ω, impedance 10 Ω
pages.why: The ohmmeter's steady current makes no back-emf, so its 6 Ω is the resistance, R. The coil's own V ÷ I is 8 Ω of inductive reactance, X_L, and the capacitor's 8 Ω of capacitive reactance, X_C. The supply's V ÷ I is the whole circuit's opposition to AC, the impedance, Z = 10 Ω, the long side of each triangle. A part's reactance comes from its own meter, not from the biggest figure, and an ohmmeter cannot see reactance at all.

pages.name: Mixed: the capacitor's meter
pages.task: Mixed. A 30 Ω resistor and a capacitor are in series on a 50 V test supply. The resistor's meter reads 30 V. What does the capacitor's meter read?
pages.why: The arrows make a right-angled triangle with the supply's 50 V as its long side, so V_C = √(50² − 30²) = √1600 = 40 V. It points down because a capacitor's voltage lags its current, but a meter reads the size of the voltage, so it shows 40 V, not −40 V. 20 V takes 30 V from 50 V as plain numbers.

pages.name: Mixed: on board ship
pages.task: Mixed. A marine college's notes (a secondary source) give 60 Hz as the frequency most common on board ship. The first bench's 6 Ω resistor and 25.5 mH coil go on a 20 V, 60 Hz supply. What current flows, and by how much does it lag?
pages.why: Only the reactance follows the frequency: X_L = 8 Ω × 60 ÷ 50 = 9.6 Ω, while R stays 6 Ω. So Z = √(6² + 9.6²) = 11.3 Ω and I = 20 ÷ 11.3 = 1.77 A, lagging by the angle whose tangent is 9.6 ÷ 6, 58.0°. 1.67 A scales the whole 10 Ω up with the frequency, resistance and all, and 2 A leaves the frequency out.
